:question/problem:
Find $(f\times g)^{′}(t)$ where

$$
f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3{t}^{2} \\ t+4 \\ 8\end{bmatrix},\,g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}t+2 \\ -2{t}^{2} \\ 5t\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Using the cross product rule, we can write:

$$
(f\times g)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times {g}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6t \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {g}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{t}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4t \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t)\times g(t) & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 6t & 1 & 0 \\ t+2 & -2{t}^{2} & 5t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2{t}^{2} & 5t\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}6t & 0 \\ t+2 & 5t\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}6t & 1 \\ t+2 & -2{t}^{2}\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ -30{t}^{2} \\ -12{t}^{3}-t-2\end{bmatrix} \\ f(t)\times {g}^{′}(t) & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 3{t}^{2} & t+4 & 8 \\ 1 & -4t & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}t+4 & 8 \\ -4t & 5\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}3{t}^{2} & 8 \\ 1 & 5\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}3{t}^{2} & t+4 \\ 1 & -4t\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}37t+20 \\ 8-15{t}^{2} \\ -12{t}^{3}-t-4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\times g)^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ -30{t}^{2} \\ -12{t}^{3}-t-2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}37t+20 \\ 8-15{t}^{2} \\ -12{t}^{3}-t-4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}42t+20 \\ 8-45{t}^{2} \\ -24{t}^{3}-2t-6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function $r(u,v)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,{v}^{2},\,4v\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface with parametrization $r(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}.$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v\operatorname{cos}⁡u)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,0,\,-4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v\operatorname{cos}⁡u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡u & 0 & -4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 0 & 2v & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 2v & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & -4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 0 & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨8{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,-4{cos}^{2}⁡u,\,2v\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the hyperbola ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 3$ in $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =(3\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}-(3\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9({sec}^{2}⁡t-{tan}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$

The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
:question/worked-solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix},\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=3,
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

A body of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}$ meters.
Find the expression for the force acting on the body at time $t.$
:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2 \\  & =2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =4\cdot (2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =8-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $2{x}^{2}\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta {e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
:question/worked-solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta {e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }+\theta {e}^{\theta }=(1+\theta ){e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\theta {e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{((1+\theta ){e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+(1+2\theta +{\theta }^{2}){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as 

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}{y+1}.
$$

Evaluate this function at the point $(\pi ,-1).$
:question/worked-solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(\pi ,-1),$ we substitute $x=\pi $ and $y=-1$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\pi ,-1) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}{y+1}{|}_{(\pi ,-1)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)}{-1+1} \\  & =\frac{-1}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.
